titulo: Depth with Three.js without freezing the page
lead: Video frames give you the film; Three.js gives you a scene drawn in code that changes angle as you scroll. The risk is the scene drawing nonstop, even when idle or off screen, and heating up the phone. Here you measure, in a headless Chromium, how many times the scene draws in each situation, and you watch the common mistake fail.
objetivo: measure a Three.js scene that only draws when the scroll changes, pauses off screen, and respects reduced motion.

aprende.t: Draw on demand: only when the scroll progress has changed
Density cap (1.5) and offscreen pause with IntersectionObserver
Count the draws with Playwright: idle, scrolling, offscreen, and reduced motion
How much Three.js weighs on the page

hero_alt: A monitor on a dark desk showing a 3D wireframe scene with geometric shapes and a perspective grid.

secoes.sub: On-demand drawing: each question is a reason NOT to draw. Click each step.

nos.detalhe: The scroll event draws nothing: it only schedules a check for the browser's next frame (requestAnimationFrame), and at most one per frame.
An IntersectionObserver tells you whether the canvas is visible. Offscreen, the check stops here: no drawing what nobody sees.
Computes the scroll progress within the scene (0 to 1). Same as the last one drawn? Stop here. Idle page = zero draws.
Positions the camera and the objects by the progress and calls renderer.render once. The kit counts it in window.__renders so the test can read it.
renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 1.5)). On a phone with density 3, drawing at 3 is four times more pixels than at 1.5, with no difference you can see while scrolling.

secoes.legenda: The common mistake is the tutorial loop: requestAnimationFrame calling render() 60 times a second, forever.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after you answer.

perguntas.p: The page is still, with the Three.js scene on screen. How many times per second should it draw?
opcoes: None: nothing changed, so there is nothing to draw.
Once per second, so it doesn't miss any change.
perguntas.explica: Draw on demand: only when the scroll progress has changed. Drawing the same image 60 times per second drains the battery and heats up the phone.

perguntas.p: On a phone with devicePixelRatio 3, the kit draws at density 1.5. Why?
opcoes: Because Three.js doesn't accept a density above 1.5 on any device.
Because the phone doesn't display density 3.
Because the canvas gets blurry above 1.5.
Because 3 gives four times the pixels of 1.5, with no visible gain.
perguntas.explica: The GPU's workload grows with the square of the density: (3 ÷ 1.5)² = 4. The cap is an engineering choice, not a library limit.

perguntas.p: The meter shows "fora da tela 85". What is missing from the page?
opcoes: Stop drawing when the canvas leaves the screen (IntersectionObserver).
Swap WebGL for a 2D canvas, which uses less GPU on a phone.
perguntas.explica: Off screen, nobody sees the drawing. The observer says when the canvas has left, and the check stops before the render.

perguntas.p: What does the kit's page do with "reduced motion" turned on?
opcoes: It draws more slowly, at 30 frames per second, to strain the eyes less.
It draws a single frame and scrolling no longer moves the scene.
It shows a notice asking the user to turn it off.
perguntas.explica: Whoever asked for less motion gets the scene still, whole. The meter checks it: reduzir 1.

itens.texto: Draws only when the progress changed and the scene is on screen.
Density up to 1.5; reduced motion = one frame.
window.__renders counted by three-medir.mjs, and the library's weight in peso.py.
